title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do \(\varepsilon _{c}>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist deciding satisfiability of every Boolean circuit with n inputs and at most cn gates in time \(O((2- \varepsilon _{c})^{n}\cdot n^{O(1)})\)?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. Circuits are finite acyclic directed graphs with input bits and one output, binary AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates; gates have unrestricted fan-out. Size counts non-input gates. The input lists every gate and predecessor index. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the n input bits makes the output one. The algorithm and the constants in its polynomial factor may depend on c, but \(\varepsilon _{c}\) must be positive and independent of n. There is no depth restriction.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive assignment search works in roughly \(2^{n}\) time regardless of circuit structure. Linear-size circuits restrict the amount of computation performed on each assignment while retaining arbitrary depth and sharing.

Obtaining a fixed exponential saving for every fixed size density would establish a general algorithmic benefit of that restriction. The question is part of the algorithms-to-lower-bounds landscape described by Wigderson. Algorithms for bounded-depth or threshold-restricted circuits do not settle the stated general model.

why: A broad satisfiability-speedup question connecting fine-grained algorithms with unrestricted circuit lower bounds.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
